hints: Do not be tricked by the $700 \mu m$ size, the large vacuole, or the cell wall. Ask yourself which one feature in the description is only ever true for one cell type.
Recall the defining difference in genetic material: prokaryotes have circular DNA free in the cytoplasm with no nucleus, while eukaryotes have linear DNA enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus.
walkthrough:
**Look Past the Misleading Clues**

Great scientists do not judge a cell by size alone. This bacterium is famously giant, but size, a vacuole for storage, and a cell wall are all found in more than one group, so they cannot prove what it is.

**Use the Defining Test for Prokaryotes**

Here is the golden rule to remember. If DNA is circular and free in the cytoplasm with no nuclear membrane around it, that is the definition of a prokaryote:
$$\text{prokaryote = circular DNA free in cytoplasm, no true nucleus}$$

**Match the Description to D**

The question tells us the DNA of T. namibiensis is circular and located free in the cytoplasm. That matches the prokaryote definition perfectly, even though the cell is huge and has a vacuole and wall.

options.A: Size is not the defining feature. T. namibiensis is an exceptionally large bacterium, but its DNA organisation still makes it a prokaryote.
options.B: A vacuole does not make it a plant. Bacteria can also have vacuoles for storage, and plant vacuoles are membrane-bound within a eukaryotic cell.
options.C: A cell wall does not make it a plant. Bacteria, fungi and plants all have cell walls, but made of different materials.
options.D: Correct. Circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm with no nucleus is the key diagnostic feature of a prokaryote.
